lines.text: Every one of these pictures started as pure random noise.
A diffusion model removes that noise one small step at a time, until a picture is left.
This is the idea behind Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Imagen and video models like Sora. Let's see how it works.
lines.speech: This is the idea behind Stable Diffusion, Dall-E, Imagen, and video models like Sora. Let's see how it works.

lines.text: Destroying a picture is easy. Add a little noise, then a little more, and after enough steps nothing is left.
The hard part is going back. A diffusion model is a network trained to undo one small step of noise.
Repeat that small step hundreds of times, starting from pure noise, and a brand-new picture appears.
The idea appeared in 2015. In 2020, Ho, Jain and Abbeel made it work on real photos. They called it DDPM.
lines.speech: The idea appeared in 2015. In 2020, Ho, Jain and Abbeel made it work on real photos. They called it D D P M.

lines.text: Here is the forward process. At each of T = 1000 steps, we shrink the image a tiny bit and add a tiny bit of Gaussian noise.
lines.speech: Here is the forward process. At each of a thousand steps, we shrink the image a tiny bit, and add a tiny bit of Gaussian noise.

lines.text: How much noise is added at each step is set by a schedule, β. In DDPM it grows from 0.0001 to 0.02.
lines.speech: How much noise is added at each step is set by a schedule, beta. In D D P M it grows from 0.0001 to 0.02.

lines.text: The nice part: we don't need to add noise step by step. We can jump straight to any step t with one formula.
xₜ is the clean image times √ᾱₜ, plus random noise ε times √(1 − ᾱₜ).
lines.speech: x t is the clean image, times the square root of alpha bar t, plus random noise, epsilon, times the square root of one minus alpha bar t.

lines.text: As t grows, the image part fades out and the noise part takes over. By step 1000, only noise is left.

scenes.title: The reverse process: a noise predictor

lines.text: Going backwards needs a neural network. It gets a noisy image xₜ and the step number t.
lines.speech: Going backwards needs a neural network. It gets a noisy image, x t, and the step number, t.

lines.text: DDPM's trick: don't ask the network for the clean image. Ask it for the noise that was added, ε.
lines.speech: D D P M's trick: don't ask the network for the clean image. Ask it for the noise that was added, epsilon.

lines.text: If you know the noise, you can remove some of it. That gives a slightly cleaner image, one step back.
Its guess of the noise also gives a guess of the clean image. Early on that guess is a blurry average. It sharpens as the noise goes away.
Training is remarkably simple. Take a clean training example.
Pick a random step t, and some random noise ε. Jump to the noisy xₜ with the formula.
lines.speech: Pick a random step, t, and some random noise, epsilon. Jump to the noisy x t with the formula.

lines.text: Ask the network to predict ε, and measure the squared error. Update, and repeat.
lines.speech: Ask the network to predict epsilon, and measure the squared error. Update, and repeat.

lines.text: That is the whole loss. There is no discriminator and no adversarial game, so training is stable, unlike a GAN.

scenes.title: Sampling: from noise to a picture

lines.text: To make a new picture, start from pure noise, and run the network once for every step, from 1000 down to 1.
At each step: predict the noise, remove a little of it, then add back a smaller amount of fresh noise.
Watch the network's guess on the right. At first it is an average of everything it knows. Then it commits to one picture.
These use the ideal denoiser for six training images, computed exactly. A trained network approximates it, and makes new pictures, not copies.

scenes.title: The network: a U-Net that knows the time

lines.text: For images, the noise predictor is usually a U-Net: the same encoder-decoder with skip connections as in Pix2Pix.
lines.speech: For images, the noise predictor is usually a U-Net: the same encoder-decoder with skip connections, as in Pix to Pix.

lines.text: Its output has the same size as its input. In goes a noisy image, out comes the predicted noise.
The step number t is turned into a vector with sines and cosines, like positions in a Transformer, and added inside every block.
So one network handles every noise level. It knows whether to remove a lot of noise or just a little.
Self-attention layers at the low resolutions let distant parts of the image agree with each other.
Newer models like Stable Diffusion 3 and Sora replace the U-Net with a Transformer. This is called a Diffusion Transformer, or DiT.
lines.speech: Newer models like Stable Diffusion 3 and Sora replace the U-Net with a Transformer. This is called a Diffusion Transformer, or D I T.

lines.text: Let's watch a real diffusion model. We trained a tiny one from scratch on 2-D points along a spiral.
Here is the forward process on that data: the spiral dissolves into a round cloud of noise.
The network is a small multi-layer perceptron. It was trained for 12,000 steps with exactly the loss we just saw.
These arrows show what it learned: at each point, which way is less noisy. With lots of noise, they point toward the middle. With little noise, they point at the spiral.
Now we sample. 1,500 points of pure noise, 1,000 steps.
The noise has become a spiral. The faint lines show the paths of a few points.
A thousand network calls per picture is slow. DDIM, from 2021, takes bigger, deterministic steps with the same trained network.
lines.speech: A thousand network calls per picture is slow. D D I M, from 2021, takes bigger, deterministic steps, with the same trained network.

lines.text: With our model, 50 steps work almost as well as 1,000. At 10 steps, most of the shape is lost. At 3 steps it falls apart.
Newer methods, like distillation and consistency models, get good images in one to four steps.
So far the model makes a random picture. To ask for something specific, we give the network a condition: a class, or a text prompt.
We trained a second tiny model on three shapes, with the shape as its condition. About one time in seven, we hid the condition, so it also learned to work without one.
Classifier-free guidance then mixes two predictions: one with the condition, one without. It pushes away from the unconditional one, by a guidance scale w.
lines.speech: Classifier-free guidance then mixes two predictions: one with the condition, and one without. It pushes away from the unconditional one, by a guidance scale, w.

lines.text: With w = 0, only the unconditional prediction is used: the samples smear across all three shapes. With w = 1, 97 percent land on the shape we asked for.
lines.speech: With w equals zero, only the unconditional prediction is used: the samples smear across all three shapes. With w equals one, 97 percent land on the shape we asked for.

lines.text: With w = 3, all of them do. But look: they cover only part of the ring, and one corner of the triangle. Stronger guidance follows the condition more closely, with less variety.
lines.speech: With w equals three, all of them do. But look: they cover only part of the ring, and one corner of the triangle. Stronger guidance follows the condition more closely, with less variety.

lines.text: Running a U-Net 50 times on a 512 by 512 image is expensive. Latent diffusion, from 2022, made it cheaper.
First, an autoencoder compresses the image into a 64 by 64 by 4 latent: 48 times fewer numbers.
Diffusion runs in that small latent space. At the end, the decoder turns the latent back into a full-size image.
The prompt goes through a text encoder, and the U-Net reads it with cross-attention. This is Stable Diffusion.
Compared with GANs from our earlier videos: diffusion trains with one simple, stable loss, and it covers the whole variety of the data instead of collapsing to a few modes.
In 2021, a paper called Diffusion Models Beat GANs showed it on ImageNet.
The price is speed: many network calls per sample instead of one. That is what DDIM, latent diffusion and distillation all fight.
Diffusion in four pieces. A forward process that adds noise, with a formula to jump to any step.
A network that predicts the noise, trained with a simple squared error.
A sampler that starts from pure noise and removes it step by step.
And conditioning with guidance, to steer it toward what you asked for.
